inventory.source_content: For a proper f:R^d→(-infinity,+infinity], g in R^d is a subgradient at x if f(y)>=f(x)+<g,y-x> for every y in R^d. The supporting inequality supplies loss divided by coordinate units for g; actual algorithm points must have finite meaningful losses.

A subgradient need not be unique; the set is denoted partial f(x), the subdifferential. Subdifferentiable at x means partial f(x) is nonempty. Therefore arbitrary independent oracle choices cannot be silently identified across runs.

inventory.region: Section2.2.3 heading and first paragraph y0.53-0.63
inventory.source_content: Actual target begins here: Unit Analysis Bits. Source warns that setting problem constants such as Lipschitz L to1 hides information needed to check equations and implement algorithms correctly.
Assign units such as meters/seconds/Joules. A physically meaningful equation must have equal units on both sides; quantities of incompatible units cannot be added.
The same dimensional sanity check is proposed for online learning: [x] denotes prediction units and [ell] loss units; terms combined in a formula must have matching units.

inventory.region: last lines continued onto printed21 y0.79-0.84
inventory.source_content: Transcendental functions take unitless arguments; logarithms/exponentials can act on ratios with matching units to yield unitless quantities. This is physical dimensional interpretation, not a prohibition on real-valued analytic functions.

Probabilities are unitless; probability density has reciprocal units of the represented random variable because it is probability per unit. Contextual rule only; no probability model enters the subsequent deterministic OSD calculation.
Source says a unit mismatch indicates an incorrect equation or a hidden unit-bearing constant, and uses dimensional analysis to constrain dependence on problem quantities.
Specialize Algorithm2.2 to V=R^d: x_(t+1)=x_t-eta g_t. Coherence requires eta g_t and x_t to have the same units. The same scalar learning rate is used in this displayed update.
From the subgradient definition the source asserts [g_t]=[ell]/[x]. Coordinates are assigned a common symbolic unit; heterogeneous coordinate scaling is not discussed.
[x_t]=[eta g_t]=[eta][g_t]. Products and quotients of symbolic units follow the displayed multiplicative convention.
[eta]=[x]/[g_t]=[x]/([ell]/[x])=[x]^2/[ell]. This is the exact dimensional relation, not a uniquely selected numerical learning rate.

Source states that the learning rate is not a unitless quantity and must depend on problem characteristics in a certain way, even before a regret guarantee is derived. The categorical unitless wording is preserved as literal claim; special dimensional cancellations are a separate qualification.

Source attributes constant-rate OSD bound to Theorem2.13: sum_(t=1)^T(ell_t(x_t)-ell_t(u)) <= ||u-x_1||_2²/(2eta)+(eta/2)sum_(t=1)^T||g_t||_2². This is the relaxed bound; full theorem retains a negative endpoint term. Comparator quantification is inherited from the theorem, for each u in V.
The left side is a sum of losses and has unit [ell]; check each right-side term has that same unit. T and numerical constants are dimensionless counts/scalars.
[||u-x_1||_2²/eta]=[x]²/[eta]=[x]²/([x]²/[ell])=[ell]. Factor2 is numerically present in the bound but unitless, so omitted only inside the unit calculation.
[eta sum_(t=1)^T||g_t||_2²]=[eta][g_t]²=([x]²/[ell])([ell]²/[x]²)=[ell]. Summands share the same unit; summation does not add a time unit.

Hidden units cause implementation problems. Let x_t represent a location in meters; choose eta=1/sqrt(T). Change measurement to kilometers: x_prime_t=x_t/1000. This retains physical location and loss-value units. The formula requires positive finite horizon for a positive finite rate.

Source says the underlying learning problem is identical because this is only a change of units, and algorithm behavior should be invariant. This expresses physical coordinate invariance, not equality of numerical coordinate vectors.

At corresponding points the source writes g_prime_t=grad_(x_prime) ell_t(1000 x_prime_t)=1000 grad_x ell_t(x_t)=1000 g_t. This example uses gradients despite the enclosing OSD discussion. The transformed loss function is z↦ell_t(1000z), with loss outputs unscaled.
Reuse the numerically unchanged eta=1/sqrt(T): x_prime_(t+1)=x_prime_t-eta g_prime_t=x_t/1000-(1/sqrt(T))(1000g_t). This calculation begins at corresponding current points.

Multiplying the new iterate by1000 gives the source displayed x_(t+1)=x_t-(1000²/sqrt(T))g_t. The unprimed x_(t+1) here names the converted NEW update; it must not be silently equated with the original algorithm update using eta.

Source says effective rate is multiplied by one million and this will drastically change the algorithm path because of a unit change. Algebra fixes the multiplier; universal strict/quantitative path change requires separate nondegeneracy qualifications.
Source attributes failure to the hidden-unit constant in the learning rate and says the rate must change when coordinate units change.

Correct eta has units [x]²/[ell] and should be scaled by (1/1000)²=1/1000000 when switching meters to kilometers. Loss units are held fixed. The source does not display a full trajectory induction or transformed regret theorem here.
Convex loss supporting inequality for every u in V.
